blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Regression fits an equation that gives the expected value of an outcome variable for given values of one or more predictor variables. Correlation measures how strongly two variables are linearly related; regression describes what the relationship is, in the units of the variables.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: A correlation coefficient answers “how strongly are these two variables related, and in which direction?” It does not answer “given this value of the predictor, what value of the outcome should I expect?” Regression answers that second question by fitting a line (or curve) through the data.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Knowing that age and weight correlate at r = 0.82 tells a clinician the relationship is strong and positive, but not what weight to expect for an 18-month-old. The regression equation for the clinic register, predicted weight = 8.5 + 0.15 × age (months), gives 11.2 kg, and §12.2.4 adds how widely individual children scatter around that prediction.

Regression to the mean. The word “regression” itself comes from a pattern every screening programme meets. Suppose adults are screened for hypertension, and everyone whose first systolic reading is 160 mmHg or more is called back for a second reading. Blood pressure varies from day to day, so a very high first reading is partly a truly high pressure and partly a high day. At the second visit the high day is not repeated on average, and the group’s mean falls, with no treatment at all.

Worked Calculation (a simulation; the values are illustrative, not survey data)

  1. Assume true systolic pressure varies between adults with mean 130 and SD 15 mmHg, and each reading adds day-to-day variation with SD 10 mmHg.
  2. Among 100,000 simulated adults, 4,825 have a first reading ≥ 160. Their mean first reading is 167.7 mmHg.
  3. The same 4,825 adults, measured again, average 156.0 mmHg: 11.7 mmHg lower, with nothing done to them.
  4. Why: the two readings share the true pressure but not the day-to-day variation, so their covariance is the true-pressure variance, 15² = 225, while each reading has variance 15² + 10² = 325 (variances of independent parts add, recall §6.5). Their correlation is 225 ÷ 325 = 0.692. §12.2.2 shows that a regression prediction lies only r times as many SDs from the mean as the predictor does. A reading 30 mmHg above the mean predicts a second reading 0.692 × 30 = 20.8 mmHg above it: 150.8 mmHg, not 160.

points.html: Correlation is symmetric: r between X and Y equals r between Y and X. Regression is directional. Regressing weight on age gives a different line from regressing age on weight, because each minimises errors in a different variable.
The weaker the correlation, the more individual points scatter around the fitted line, and the less precise predictions for individuals become. The equation can still be calculated.

Regression to the mean occurs whenever people are selected because of an extreme first measurement and then measured again. It makes natural variation look like real change, and it is larger when measurement error is larger (Barnett, van der Pols & Dobson, 2005). A before–after study of “patients with high BP at screening” will show a fall even if the intervention does nothing. The defences are a randomised control group, which regresses equally, and basing selection on the mean of two or more readings.
